question: What obstacle clearance requirement applies to the take-off climb of a single-engine Class B aeroplane?

options.text: A 50 ft vertical margin up to 1 500 ft
None is set by the operating rules
A 35 ft vertical margin up to 1 500 ft

explanation: The operating rules set no obstacle clearance limit for single-engine Class B aeroplanes. Other classes must clear obstacles by 50 ft or 35 ft.

question: Why is there no regulatory obstacle clearance requirement for a single-engine Class B aeroplane?

options.text: Obstacles are always cleared by the 50 ft screen height
The aeroplane never flies near obstacles
The pilot must always be able to see and avoid obstacles

explanation: The pilot must keep visual contact with the ground, so obstacles in the take-off path can be seen and avoided. A clearance calculation is still prudent where obstacles are known.

question: What minimum climb gradient do the operating rules require of a single-engine Class B aeroplane after take-off?
explanation: There is no operational minimum climb gradient. The 4% all-engines gradient is a multi-engine Class B requirement.

question: Why is no operational minimum climb gradient set for single-engine Class B aeroplanes?

options.text: The aeroplanes cannot climb steeply enough to meet one anyway
They only fly at low altitude

explanation: The certification specifications for this type of aeroplane are stringent enough on their own, so no further operational gradient is imposed.

question: Even without a regulatory climb requirement, why should the pilot know the expected climb performance?

options.text: To report it to ATC before departure
Because it must be entered on the load sheet for the flight
To be sure it can climb adequately

explanation: Operating with performance so poor that the aeroplane can barely climb would not be safe, so the pilot should know the climb that will be achieved.

question: Which conditions does a typical single-engine climb graph assume?

options.text: Full throttle, mixture rich, flaps and gear up
Idle power and flaps fully down
Take-off flap and gear down, cowl flaps closed

explanation: A typical climb graph assumes full throttle, rich mixture, flaps and gear up and cowl flaps as required, at a stated climb IAS.

question: What are the two main uses of the climb graph?

options.text: Stall speed, and best glide speed
Fuel for the cruise, and landing distance
Time to climb, and gradient for ground distance or obstacles

explanation: The graph gives the climb gradient or rate of climb, used to find the time to climb to cruise and, with a wind correction, ground distances and obstacle clearance.

question: The climb graph makes no correction for wind. When must its gradient be corrected for wind?

options.text: For every use of the graph
For time-to-climb calculations to the cruise level

explanation: Obstacle clearance and ground distance use ground gradients, which depend on wind. Time to climb depends only on rate of climb, which wind does not affect.

question: What is the maximum mass for a required climb gradient, as found from a climb graph, also called?
explanation: The greatest mass that still gives a required gradient, such as 4%, depends on weight (mass), altitude and temperature and is called the WAT or MAT limit.

question: An aeroplane climbs at 600 ft/min. How long does it take to climb 6 000 ft?
explanation: Time = height ÷ rate of climb = 6 000 ÷ 600 = 10 minutes. Wind does not affect this.

question: An aeroplane has a rate of climb of 500 ft/min at a ground speed of 100 kt. What is its ground gradient?
A single-engine aeroplane climbs at a 6% ground gradient from the 50 ft screen. What ground distance does it need to reach 1 500 ft above reference zero?
explanation: Height to gain = 1 450 ft; distance = 1 450 ÷ 6 × 100 ≈ 24 170 ft. Ignoring the screen height gives 25 000 ft.

question: A single-engine aeroplane climbs at 100 KIAS. Why might its TAS be needed to use the climb graph?

options.text: The graph is entered with the ground speed only, never IAS
TAS gives the time to climb

explanation: Converting a rate of climb to a gradient needs the true speed through the air (or ground speed for a ground gradient), so the IAS must be converted to TAS.

question: An aeroplane with a 5% climb gradient flies over an obstacle 2 NM beyond reference zero. How high is it above reference zero? (1 NM = 6 080 ft; screen 50 ft)
explanation: 2 NM = 12 160 ft; 5% of 12 160 = 608 ft; add the 50 ft screen: about 658 ft, roughly 660 ft.
